To fix (2)

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 7 imprecise p values out of 29 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
ps > .690 Neither dogmatic intolerance nor authoritarianism was associated with the model-agnostic learning rate (all ps > .690).
ps ≤ .006 In the all-outlier-exclusion analyses, inverse associations emerged for both factors in controls-adjusted and unadjusted specifications (all ps ≤ .006).
ps ≥ .326 Learning-rate associations remained null across all available control variables and outlier-exclusion analyses (all ps ≥ .326; Supplementary Table S6).
ps ≥ .577 Neither factor moderated the relationship between prediction error and confidence, indicating no evidence that metacognitive sensitivity varied as a function of either factor (all ps ≥ .577; Supplementary Table S7).
ps ≥ .584 The same conclusion was obtained with this specification (all ps ≥ .584; Supplementary Table S7).
ps ≥ .260 Authoritarianism was not reliably associated with any fitted HGF parameter in either controls-adjusted (all ps ≥ .260) or control-free full-sample models (all ps ≥ .121; Table 2; Supplementary Tables S8-S9).
ps ≥ .121 Authoritarianism was not reliably associated with any fitted HGF parameter in either controls-adjusted (all ps ≥ .260) or control-free full-sample models (all ps ≥ .121; Table 2; Supplementary Tables S8-S9).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To fix Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed 7 R code files for reproducibility and ran 5 of them (each in an isolated Docker container).
  • 3 of 5 scripts ran without error when executed (1 more is run by another script with source()).
  • Of the others, 1 did not reproduce and 1 did not finish within the time limit.
  • 22 installable dependencies detected.
  • Metacheck detected version information that can be used to install specific versions of software for the reproducibility run. We recommend retrying the reproducibility check with recorded_versions = TRUE. This will install the required R packages, if still available. As this takes a long time, this setting is not implemented on this shared server.
  • 2126 statistics stored from the extracted output; 0 of 26 reported tests matched (0%).

To check (5)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 10 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .143 The corresponding association for authoritarianism was not significant (p = .143).
ps > .690 Neither dogmatic intolerance nor authoritarianism was associated with the model-agnostic learning rate (all ps > .690).
p = .106 In the controlfree full sample, mean-inference accuracy was inversely associated with authoritarianism (β = -.021, p = .038) but not dogmatic intolerance (β = -.017, p = .106).
ps ≥ .326 Learning-rate associations remained null across all available control variables and outlier-exclusion analyses (all ps ≥ .326; Supplementary Table S6).
ps ≥ .577 Neither factor moderated the relationship between prediction error and confidence, indicating no evidence that metacognitive sensitivity varied as a function of either factor (all ps ≥ .577; Supplementary Table S7).
ps ≥ .584 The same conclusion was obtained with this specification (all ps ≥ .584; Supplementary Table S7).
p = .157 Dogmatic intolerance was not reliably associated with the tonic-volatility parameter (ω) or the variancevolatility parameter (ωα) in the primary controls-adjusted model (p = .157 and p = .942).
p = .942 Dogmatic intolerance was not reliably associated with the tonic-volatility parameter (ω) or the variancevolatility parameter (ωα) in the primary controls-adjusted model (p = .157 and p = .942).
ps ≥ .260 Authoritarianism was not reliably associated with any fitted HGF parameter in either controls-adjusted (all ps ≥ .260) or control-free full-sample models (all ps ≥ .121; Table 2; Supplementary Tables S8-S9).
ps ≥ .121 Authoritarianism was not reliably associated with any fitted HGF parameter in either controls-adjusted (all ps ≥ .260) or control-free full-sample models (all ps ≥ .121; Table 2; Supplementary Tables S8-S9).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

To check Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 28 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 2 of 425 data columns (0%) are documented in a codebook; 423 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (28 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents subject_id, Stage, ID while the data has subject_id, Mean, Angle. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 1 codebook/README/label source and 425 data columns across 10 files.

A codebook was found and parsed (28 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents subject_id, Stage, ID while the data has subject_id, Mean, Angle. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

Careless Responding

98 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

What this does not cover. Only 2 of 10 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 5 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. Metacheck detected version information that can be used to install specific versions of software for the reproducibility run. We recommend retrying the reproducibility check with recorded_versions = TRUE. This will install the required R packages, if still available. As this takes a long time, this setting is not implemented on this shared server.

3 of 5 scripts ran to the end: 1 did not reproduce, and 1 did not finish within our time limit.

02 Data Checks.Rmd Ran to the end
03 Descriptives.Rmd Ran to the end

helper_functions.R Ran inside another script Another script runs it with source(), so it ran as part of that script.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • 05 Main analyses.Rmd

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 7 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis

4 04 Factor and composite scores.Rmd 01 Preprocessing.qmd dependency
5 helper_functions.R — none
6 05 Main analyses.Rmd 01 Preprocessing.qmd, helper_functions.R dependency

File paths

6 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: /questionnaire_data.csv to ../../data/L122136/questionnaire_data.csv (in 01 Preprocessing.qmd); /mood_data.csv to ../../data/L122136/mood_data.csv (in 01 Preprocessing.qmd); /cleaned/questionnaire_clean.csv to ../../data/L122136/cleaned/questionnaire_clean.csv (in 02 Data Checks.Rmd); /cleaned/task_clean.csv to ../../data/L122136/cleaned/task_clean.csv (in 03 Descriptives.Rmd); /cleaned/questionnaire_clean.csv to ../../data/L122136/cleaned/questionnaire_clean.csv (in 03 Descriptives.Rmd); questionnaire_clean.csv to ../../data/L122136/cleaned/questionnaire_clean.csv (in 04 Factor and composite scores.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.

Files not run on their own

2 files only define functions, so running them on their own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 1 is used by no script in the deposit.

helper_functions.R 01 Preprocessing.qmd, 02 Data Checks.Rmd, 05 Main analyses.Rmd
ModelEstimationWrapper.R no script

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 6 scripts: 3 ran without error, 1 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

Other changes we made to run the code

Stan files in the syntax Stan removed in version 2.33 were given the newer syntax, and Git LFS pointers (placeholders a GitHub archive holds instead of the file) were replaced by the deposit’s copy of the file. Updating the Stan files, and depositing the files themselves, solves this.

File Change
code/R/models/ehgf_jget_full.stan Stan from before 2.33: array declarations

Calls that install packages in the code

3 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Run by another script

1 script is run by another script with source(), so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script’s outcome.

> rownames(items_df) <- questionnaire$subject_id

> composites_df <- items_df %>%

>   ) %>%
>   select(

> scale_items <- list(
>   DOG  = c("dogx", "dogz", paste0("dog", 1:20)),
>   RWA  = paste0("rwa", 1:12),
>   LWA  = paste0("lwa", 1:8),
>   SECS = paste0("secs", 1:12),
>   PI   = c("pi1_health", "pi2_immi", "pi3_abort", "pi4_need", "pi5_id",
>            "pi6_tax", "pi7_tort", "pi8_aff", "pi9_rel"),
>   BS   = c("bs1_health", "bs2_immi", "bs3_abort", "bs4_need", "bs5_id",
>            "bs6_tax", "bs7_tort", "bs8_aff", "bs9_rel"),
>   LC   = c("lc_gen", "lc_eco", "lc_soc"),
>   CM   = paste0("cm", 1:5),
>   IUS  = paste0("ius", 1:12)
> )
> scale_items <- lapply(scale_items, function(x) x[x %in% names(questionnaire)])
> scale_properties <- function(data, items, scale_name) {
>   
>   dat_items <- data %>%
>     select(all_of(items)) %>%
>     mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))
>   
>   scale_score <- rowMeans(dat_items, na.rm = TRUE)
>   scale_score[rowSums(!is.na(dat_items)) == 0] <- NA
>   
>   alpha_val <- if (length(items) >= 2) {
>     tryCatch(
>       psych::alpha(dat_items, warnings = FALSE, check.keys = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha,
>       error = function(e) NA_real_
>     )
>   } else {
>     NA_real_
>   }
>   
>   omega_val <- if (length(items) >= 3) {
>     tryCatch(
>       psych::omega(dat_items, nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE, warnings = FALSE)$omega.tot,
>       error = function(e) NA_real_
>     )
>   } else {
>     NA_real_
>   }
>   
>   mean_interitem_r <- if (length(items) >= 2) {
>     cors <- cor(dat_items, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
>     mean(cors[upper.tri(cors)], na.rm = TRUE)
>   } else {
>     NA_real_
>   }
>   
>   tibble(
>     scale = scale_name,
>     n_items = length(items),
>     n_complete = sum(complete.cases(dat_items)),
>     mean = mean(scale_score, na.rm = TRUE),
>     sd = sd(scale_score, na.rm = TRUE),
>     min = min(scale_score, na.rm = TRUE),
>     max = max(scale_score, na.rm = TRUE),
>     alpha = alpha_val,
>     omega_total = omega_val,
>     mean_interitem_r = mean_interitem_r
>   )
> }
> scale_props <- bind_rows(
>   lapply(names(scale_items), function(scale_name) {
>     scale_properties(
>       data = questionnaire,
>       items = scale_items[[scale_name]],
>       scale_name = scale_name
>     )
>   })
> )
> scale_props %>%

>   item_labels <- c(

>         item == "LWA"  ~ "LWA",
>         item == "SECS" ~ "SECS",
>         item == "PI"   ~ "Political issues",
>         item == "BS"   ~ "Belief superiority"

>       item_label = recode(item, !!!item_labels),

>     scale_fill_manual(values = scale_colours, name = NULL) +

> plot_efa3_loadings <- function(
>     fit_efa_3,

>   item_labels <- c(
>     "lc_gen"   = "General ideology",

>     "Belief superiority", "Dogmatism"
>   )
>   group_sizes <- c(3, 2, 6)
>   sep_y <- length(item_order) - cumsum(group_sizes)[-length(group_sizes)] + 0.5
> 
>   loading_long <- lavaan::standardizedSolution(fit_efa_3, type = "std.all") %>%
>     filter(op == "=~") %>%

> 
>   stopifnot(all(loading_long$item_label %in% item_order))
>

>   if (!is.null(factor_labels)) {
>     lab <- factor_labels[factor_order]

> 
>   fills <- factor_cols[factor_order]

>   names(fills) <- factor_order
> 
>   loading_long %>%
>     mutate(
>       item_label = factor(item_label, levels = item_order),
>       factor     = factor(factor, levels = factor_order),
>       is_salient = abs(loading) >= salient,
>       lab        = fmt_loading(loading),
>       lab_col    = if_else(is_salient, ink, muted)
>     ) %>%
>     ggplot(aes(x = loading, y = item_label, fill = factor)) +
>     geom_hline(yintercept = sep_y, colour = rule, linewidth = 0.3) +

>     {

>         )

> bucket_size <- 36
> data <- data %>%
>   mutate(
>     Std = if_else(Noise_Condition == "Low_Noise",12,21),
>     # Signed circular distance between bucket centre and latent mean
>     delta = ((Bucket.Position - Mean + 180) %% 360) - 180,
> 
>     # Theoretical probability of catching the particle
>     P_catch = round(
>       pnorm((delta + bucket_size / 2) / Std) -
>       pnorm((delta - bucket_size / 2) / Std),
>       4
>       ),
>     calibration = conf/100 - P_catch,
>     overconf = as.numeric(calibration > 0)
>   ) %>% select(
>     -c(Std,delta,P_catch)
>   )

Ethics Approval Check

The paper appears to report data that the authors collected from people or animals, and it has an ethics statement.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
