Dogmatic intolerance is associated with a more changeable representation of environmental volatility (ϑ).

To examine whether the behavioral findings were reflected in participants' computational representations of the task, we next tested whether radical-attitude factors were associated with fitted HGF parameters. Whereas mean inference and confidence capture observed task behavior, the HGF parameters index latent assumptions governing belief updating. Higher dogmatic intolerance was associated with higher values of the environmental-volatility parameter (ϑ), β = .100, 95% CI [.007, .192], t(443) = 2.12, p = .034 (Fig. 4B). This parameter governs how readily the model allows the volatility of the latent mean itself to change over time. The association remained in the control-free full-sample (β = .094, p = .044), control-free all-outlier (β = .099, p = .034), and controls-adjusted all-outlier analyses (β = .105, p = .026), indicating that the association was robust across these analytical specifications. Dogmatic intolerance was not reliably associated with the tonic-volatility parameter (ω) or the variancevolatility parameter (ωα) in the primary controls-adjusted model (p = .157 and p = .942). Authoritarianism was not reliably associated with any fitted HGF parameter in either controls-adjusted (all ps ≥ .260) or control-free full-sample models (all ps ≥ .121; Table 2; Supplementary Tables S8-S9). No outliers were identified for authoritarianism.

DISCUSSION

Previous research has linked radical attitudes to reduced cognitive flexibility and altered belief updating (Kossowska et al., 2026; Schumann et al., 2022; Sinclair et al., 2020; Zmigrod et al., 2019 Zmigrod et al., , 2020)). The observation that such associations also emerge in tasks stripped of ideology-laden content suggests a bias in domain-general cognitive processes. However, similar behavioral patterns may arise from distinct computational mechanisms underlying decision-making, which remain poorly understood in relation to radical attitudes. Here, we used a predictive inference task with a previously validated computational model that jointly estimates learning about the latent state, environmental volatility, and observational noise (Mikuš et al., 2025) to examine whether radical attitudes are associated with distinct behavioral and computational characteristics of belief updating under uncertainty. We found weak effects of radical attitudes on general task performance and no support for an association with metacognitive sensitivity. By contrast, both dogmatic intolerance and authoritarianism were associated with overconfidence, while dogmatic intolerance was additionally associated with a higher environmental-volatility parameter (ϑ).

The model-agnostic analyses provided limited evidence for associations between radical attitudes and inference accuracy or belief updating. Dogmatic intolerance was weakly associated with poorer mean inference in controls-adjusted analyses, but not in models without control variables. After excluding outliers, negative associations emerged for both dogmatic intolerance and authoritarianism.

Neither factor was associated with the model-agnostic learning rate. By contrast, both radical-attitude factors were associated with higher confidence after accounting for task performance, as well as greater overconfidence, defined as the proportion of trials on which reported confidence exceeded the theoretical probability of success. This pattern is broadly consistent with previous findings linking dogmatism to higher self-assessed performance (Binnendyk & Pennycook, 2024) and authoritarianism to elevated confidence or perceived ability (Choma et al., 2019; Sinclair et al., 2020). However, other studies found no general confidence bias associated with dogmatism (Rollwage et al., 2018; Schulz et al., 2020). We also found no evidence that radical attitudes moderate the relationship between preceding prediction errors and subsequent confidence, even when catch outcomes were used as an alternative performance measure. This differs from Rollwage et al. (2018), who reported reduced metacognitive sensitivity using meta-d′, although their measure captures the ability to distinguish correct from incorrect decisions through confidence judgments, rather than confidence adjustments following prediction errors.

These differences may partly reflect the distinct task structures and measures employed (Fleming & Lau, 2014). Whereas Rollwage et al. (2018) and Schulz et al. (2020) used binary perceptual decision designs, our task involved continuous predictions in a changing environment. Moreover, unlike Schulz et al. (2020), we used a finer-grained confidence scale and financially incentivized confidence ratings.

Our findings suggest that elevated subjective certainty associated with radical attitudes extends beyond political belief evaluation, without necessarily being accompanied by impaired learning. This pattern is consistent with computational accounts in which confidence judgments rely on processes partially distinct from those supporting first-order cognition (Fleming & Daw, 2017). However, elevated confidence may still influence subsequent belief updating by shaping how individuals seek and process information.

Experimental work has shown that higher confidence reduces changes of mind by selectively amplifying the processing of choice-consistent evidence while attenuating the influence of disconfirmatory evidence (Rollwage et al., 2020). Similarly, Schulz et al. (2020) found that dogmatic individuals relied less on low confidence as a signal to seek additional information, suggesting differences in how confidence guides information search. These findings suggest that the consequences of overconfidence may depend on whether, and under what conditions, subjective certainty influences subsequent information processing. In our task, evidence was externally provided on every trial, limiting opportunities for confidence to influence information selection or avoidance, although differences in evidence weighting remained possible. The consequences of overconfidence for belief updating may become more apparent in complex, real-world environments, where individuals can selectively seek or avoid information. At the same time, even small differences in information processing could accumulate over extended periods and shape more complex beliefs (Rollwage et al., 2018). Whether the overconfidence observed here contributes to such cumulative effects over time remains an open question for future research.

At the computational level, the pattern was more specific to dogmatic intolerance. Using a computational model that jointly estimated environmental volatility (ϑ), learning about observational noise (ωα) and the tonic volatility (ω), we found that dogmatic intolerance was associated selectively with higher values of perceived environmental volatility (ϑ), indicating greater changeability in beliefs about how stable or unstable the underlying environment is over time. This association was consistent across sensitivity analyses. By contrast, dogmatic intolerance was not associated with tonic volatility (ω), or with variance volatility (ωα). This distinction is important because learning about environmental change and responding to individual unexpected observations involve separable, though interacting, computational processes (Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2010; Piray & Daw, 2021). Previous work using a similar task and the same model showed that higher environmental volatility ϑ was linked to higher coupling of prediction errors and confidence (i.e., metacognitive sensitivity) as well as to a higher likelihood of experiencing delusional thought patterns (Mikuš et al., 2025). One possible interpretation is that greater changeability in representations of environmental volatility allows individuals to accommodate unexpected information by revising assumptions about the environment rather than their existing beliefs. Computational accounts suggest that such adjustments to peripheral explanations can preserve central beliefs despite contradictory evidence, allowing flexibility in interpreting new information to coexist with rigidity in established convictions (Erdmann & Mathys, 2022; Gershman, 2019).

The possibility that individuals may revise their explanations of the environment while preserving central beliefs also raises the question of why maintaining these beliefs might be important. Theories of epistemic closure suggest that firm convictions can provide a sense of stability when uncertainty is experienced as aversive (Webster & Kruglanski, 1994; Kruglanski & Webster, 1996; Kruglanski et al., 2006). Consistent with this perspective, previous research has linked dogmatism to intolerance of uncertainty (Kossowska et al., 2017). Our interpretations here are, however, necessarily tentative and longitudinal studies would be needed to determine the causal direction of the relationship between a more changeable representation of environmental volatility and dogmatic worldviews.

There are several limitations to consider. First, conceptualizing radical attitudes remains a longstanding challenge (Borum, 2011; Jungkunz et al., 2024; Knorr & Kossowska, 2025; Knorr et al., 2026; Sedgwick, 2010). Although we included multiple measures, no selection of indicators fully captures their diversity, and measurement choices may influence observed associations. We focused our analyses on attitudinal dimensions because these dimensions concern how individuals hold and evaluate beliefs and respond to disagreement, making them particularly relevant to the processes of belief formation and revision examined here. This choice necessarily limits the scope of our conclusions. Future research should examine whether our findings extend to other types of radical commitment. Second, although both radical-attitude dimensions were associated with overconfidence, this was not accompanied by consistent differences in belief updating. The task involved repeated exposure to externally generated evidence over 300 trials but did not allow participants to determine which information to seek or avoid.

This distinction may be consequential because overconfidence could influence learning particularly when subjective certainty guides information selection, evaluation, or decisions about whether further evidence is needed. Moreover, the relatively short timescale and simplified structure of the task may have limited our ability to detect cumulative effects of confidence-related biases. Future studies should therefore examine how confidence influences belief updating in long-term designs. Third, our study was conducted online, which limited control over participants' testing environments and may have introduced additional noise in measurement. Nevertheless, previous research suggests that online cognitive experiments can yield valid results, even when the data are noisier than those collected under laboratory conditions (Crump et al., 2013; Germine et al., 2012). Fourth, the analyses were exploratory and addressed several related but theoretically distinct research questions. We did not apply a blanket multiple-testing correction, as our aim was to examine individual associations between radical attitudes and different aspects of predictive inference. As argued by García-Pérez (2023), multiple-testing adjustments should reflect the substantive inferences being drawn rather than simply the number of statistical tests performed. Finally, although our task builds on established approaches to predictive inference and learning under uncertainty (Loosen et al., 2024; Nassar et al., 2010; Seow & Gillan, 2020; Vaghi et al., 2017), its specific structure and computational assumptions may have influenced the findings. Independent replication, ideally across different task implementations, is therefore needed to establish their reliability and generalizability.

To conclude, both dogmatic intolerance and authoritarianism were associated with overconfidence in a politically neutral predictive-inference task, without evidence of reduced metacognitive sensitivity. Beyond these confidence differences, our computational analyses revealed a selective association between dogmatic intolerance and the representation of environmental volatility (ϑ). At first glance, these findings suggest an intriguing contrast: greater certainty in one's own judgments alongside a more changeable representation of the environment. Yet these tendencies may be connected, as attributing unexpected outcomes to changes in the environment rather than to inaccuracies in one's own judgments could help sustain subjective confidence. By pointing to a higherorder computational correlate of dogmatic intolerance, our study extends research on radical attitudes beyond observable cognitive performance and offers a new perspective on how basic representations of uncertainty may relate to dogmatic-intolerant worldviews.

Figure 2.

Figure 2. Computational model. (A) Observations are drawn from a changing Gaussian distribution with varying variance. Participants form predictions and update their beliefs about the underlying states based on prediction errors. The size of these updates depends on the precision weight ψ₁, defined as the ratio of estimated outcome precision (πu) to expected mean precision (πx). Expected mean precision, in turn, depends on uncertainty about the mean (σx) and beliefs about volatility (μv). (B) The generative model contains two parallel cascades of Gaussian random walks: one describing changes in the mean (x) and its log-volatility (xv), and one describing changes in outcome variance (xα), also on the log scale. (C) Model inversion using the hierarchical Gaussian filter provides estimates of the mean and precision of beliefs about the latent mean, variance, and volatility. Reproduced without modification from Mikuš et al. (2025) under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0).

Figure 3.

Figure 3. Factor structure. Standardized factor loadings from the retained three-factor exploratory factor analysis of six scale composites and five individual items, estimated using robust maximum likelihood with geomin oblique rotation. Bars show standardized loadings, with darker colors indicating absolute loadings ≥ .30 and lighter colors indicating loadings below this threshold. Note. SECS = Social and Economic Conservatism Scale; RWA = right-wing authoritarianism; LWA = left-wing authoritarianism. Dogmatic intolerance is weakly associated with less accurate mean inference.

Figure 4.

Figure 4. Associations of radical attitudes with behavioral and computational measures of predictive inference. (A) Standardized regression coefficients (dots) and 95% confidence intervals (horizontal lines) for associations of dogmatic intolerance and authoritarianism with behavioral measures of predictive inference. Confidence coefficients are adjusted for prediction error, whereas metacognitive sensitivity is represented by the interaction between radical-attitude factors and prediction error. (B) Associations between the environmental-volatility parameter (ϑ) and radical-attitude factor scores. Each dot represents one participant. Regression lines show the controls-adjusted slopes, with standardized coefficients (β) and p values indicated. All regression models were adjusted for age, gender, and education (N = 448).

Table 2 . Radical-attitude factors and fitted HGF parameters

Note. Primary covariate-adjusted linear models (N = 448). All variables were standardized; covariates included age, gender, and education. * p < .05. All tests are two-sided.
